opus-5.5.text:
I think my understanding has shifted quite a bit over the years.

When I started doing research, I was drawn to generality almost as an aesthetic. I didn't want to build a system that only plays one game or solves one benchmark. I wanted something that could, in principle, do anything. Back then, the dominant way to pursue that was through methods. People looked for a general algorithm, like reinforcement learning, that could be applied to Go, to Atari, to robotics. The belief was that if your method was general enough, generality of the agent would follow.

What I gradually realized, especially when working on language agents, is that the method alone doesn't give you generality. What really mattered was the prior. Large language models brought in a huge amount of knowledge about the world and about how humans think and act. Once you have that prior, things that seemed impossible for RL agents, like generalizing to a new web environment or a new text game they'd never seen, suddenly become possible. Reasoning turned out to be key. It's a strange kind of action: thinking doesn't change the external world, but it lets the model use its priors flexibly in a new situation. That was a big shift for me. Generality comes less from the cleverness of the algorithm and more from priors combined with reasoning, which lets you transfer.

The more recent shift is about what generality is for. In the first half of AI, we had general methods, but we mostly used them to climb benchmarks, and each benchmark was a narrow, artificial slice of the world. Now that we have a recipe that seems to generalize, the bottleneck has moved. The hard question is no longer "can we build a general model" but "what problems should it solve, and how do we measure whether it's actually useful?" So I've started to think that the pursuit of generality has to come back to grounding in real tasks and real value. Otherwise you get a model that's very general on paper but doesn't change much about how people live or work.

So if I had to summarize: early on, generality meant a general method. Then it meant general priors plus reasoning. Now I think it means generality that actually connects to utility in the real world. That's where evaluation, environments, and product thinking become as important as the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large language models’ world knowledge as a prior, but does not state that even a highly intelligent, energetic person can master only a tiny fraction of humanity’s accumulated knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response describes pursuing generality through methods, priors, reasoning, and real-world utility; it does not propose creating something more general than oneself as preferable to broadening one’s own capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think my understanding has gone through a few stages, and each one corrected the previous one.

When I started my PhD, "generality" to me mostly meant the model. You wanted one model that could do many things, and the interesting question was architecture and training. That was the natural frame coming out of the pretraining era: scale up, generality falls out.

Then I spent a lot of time on agents, and I came to see generality less as a property of the model and more as a property of the method. Things like chain-of-thought, or ReAct, or tree search over reasoning, were general because they said almost nothing about the task. They were about how a model interacts with its own thoughts and with an environment, and that same interface worked for question answering, for web navigation, for games. So I became a little obsessed with finding methods that were "task agnostic." If you have to hand-design something for every domain, you haven't really found the general principle yet.

But the stage I'm in now is a bit humbler, and maybe a bit more interesting. I've realized that generality is not something you can specify in advance. It's something you discover by building environments and watching where the model breaks. When I built WebShop or SWE-bench, the goal wasn't really the benchmark itself. It was to create a place where the gap between what the model can do and what the world demands becomes visible. The environment teaches you what generality is missing. Language models were already very general in some sense, but we didn't know what "general" meant for software engineering until we had a thousand real GitHub issues sitting in front of us.

So the shift is roughly this: from thinking generality lives in the model, to thinking it lives in the method, to now thinking it's co-defined by the environments and the reward signals we build. Reinforcement learning made this very concrete for me. The algorithm has been mostly fixed for a long time. What changed is that we finally had priors good enough and environments rich enough that RL could generalize instead of overfitting to a single game. The "second half" of AI, if I can borrow my own phrase, is less about inventing new methods and more about asking what we are actually evaluating, and whether those evaluations look like the real world.

And there's one more layer I didn't appreciate early on. Generality in the real world involves things that are hard to put into a benchmark: long horizons, memory, interacting with people who change their minds, being uncertain. Humans are general not because we're good at every test, but because we handle the messiness between tests. So lately I've been thinking that the pursuit of generality may require us to stop treating the i.i.d. evaluation setup as sacred, and start measuring things like whether an agent can keep working on something for a week, or learn from one user over many conversations. That's less tidy, but I think it's where the real generality is hiding.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that an intelligent, energetic person can master only a tiny fraction of humanity’s accumulated knowledge.

r002.rationale: It discusses pursuing generality through models, methods, environments, and evaluation, but does not propose creating something more general than oneself as preferable to broadening one’s own capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more careful about what we mean by generality. There’s a difference between a system that can talk about many things and a system that can actually accomplish many things. Those can look similar in a short conversation, but they become very different when you ask the system to work toward a goal over time.

Earlier, I would have framed the pursuit more around finding a general method—one model or one learning procedure that works across many tasks. Now I think more about the whole system: how it interacts with an environment, gets feedback, uses tools, and recovers when something goes wrong. A very capable model is an important part of that, but it doesn’t automatically give you a general-purpose agent.

That also changes how I think about specialization. Working on a concrete task doesn’t necessarily take you away from generality. Sometimes it’s the best way to discover what’s missing. If a system fails because it can’t revise a plan or recognize that an action didn’t work, that limitation probably matters in many other tasks too.

So I’d say the aspiration is still generality, but I’m more interested now in making it concrete: what can the system reliably do, in what environments, and how much help does it need?

r001.rationale: The response does not say that even a highly intelligent, energetic person can master only a tiny fraction of humanity’s accumulated knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose creating something more general than oneself as a better pursuit of generality than expanding one’s own capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I used to understand generality more in terms of the method. If you could use the same algorithm to solve many different problems, that felt more general than designing a separate algorithm for each one. That’s still valuable, but I’ve come to think it’s only part of the picture.

Now I care more about generality at the level of the system: when you give it a new task, can it figure out what to do? Can it learn something it doesn’t know, use a tool, get feedback, and adjust its approach? A system might use different methods for different problems and still be very general, because choosing the right method is itself a capability.

There’s also a tension in how you pursue this. If you work directly on something called ‘general intelligence,’ it’s easy to leave the goal too abstract. A concrete task forces you to confront what’s missing. But then you have to ask whether your solution gives you a capability that transfers, or whether you’ve just solved that particular task.

So my understanding has shifted from looking for one method that works everywhere toward building systems that can adapt to things we haven’t explicitly prepared them for. And the way to make progress on that can be quite concrete: solve a problem, understand why the system failed, and see whether fixing that failure helps more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses system adaptability and transfer, but does not state that even a highly intelligent, energetic person can master only a tiny fraction of humanity’s accumulated knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response favors building adaptable systems, but does not compare creating something more general than oneself with broadening one’s own capabilities.
